claims.text: The catalyst's excellent ethanol-oxidation performance is controlled by potential-induced, reversible formation of surface oxide species.
Transient surface oxide layers alter the catalyst's d-band structure.
Changes in d-band structure tune the adsorption energies of ethanol and its intermediates.
The adsorption-energy changes facilitate the electron-proton transfers required for ethanol oxidation.
The initial catalyst is Pt-rich and predominantly metallic, without significant surface oxide.
Low applied potentials favor a metallic catalyst surface, whereas high potentials favor oxide formation.
Surface oxide layers such as PtOx form and reduce dynamically during potential stepping.
Partial and reversible surface oxidation produces a downshift in the d-band center.
The oxide-induced electronic modulation adjusts the binding energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Partial reversible oxidation boosts both catalytic activity and durability.
Excessive oxidation deactivates active sites and reduces performance.
An optimal potential range will exist in which dynamic oxide formation coincides with peak ethanol-oxidation current and selectivity.
Predominantly metallic and extensively oxidized surface states will both exhibit lower activity and selectivity than the dynamic, partially oxidized state.
A steady potential can maintain a predominantly metallic baseline surface.
The proposed mechanism applies only when surface oxidation is reversible and sensitive to applied potential.
Catalysts lacking reversible surface oxidation, or operated under substantially different electrolyte conditions, may not show the proposed performance dependence.
Operando XAS can quantify oxidation-state evolution while cyclic voltammetry and product analysis track activity and selectivity.
